Giant Squid.
For centuries, the giant squid was known mostly from dead ones washing ashore and from sailors' stories,
and nobody had ever filmed one alive down where it actually lives.
That changed in July twenty twelve, when a Japanese team led by zoologist Tsunemi Kubodera took a submersible down near the Ogasawara Islands,

At about six hundred and thirty meters, a giant squid finally showed up,
and they followed it down to roughly nine hundred meters. The animal was about three meters long.
What makes it unsettling is the eyes.
A giant squid eye has been measured at about twenty-seven centimeters across, roughly the size of a basketball.
The pupil alone is about nine centimeters wide, big enough to fit the entire eye of a swordfish inside it.
Only its cousin, the colossal squid, has eyes to rival it.

Barreleye Fish.
Look at its face and you'll see two small dark spots above the mouth, staring back at you.
Those aren't its eyes.
They're its nostrils, and the real eyes are inside its head.
The barreleye lives about six hundred to eight hundred meters down in the North Pacific, and it's only about fifteen centimeters long.
The top of its head is a transparent, fluid-filled shield, like a see-through phone case,

For decades after the species was first described in nineteen thirty-nine, scientists believed those eyes were fixed in place,
pointing straight up and giving the fish permanent tunnel vision.
Most specimens came up in nets, and the delicate shield didn't survive the trip,

Here's the part that surprised everyone.
When researchers at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute finally watched living barreleyes with underwater robots,

The fish hangs motionless in the dark with its eyes pointed up, watching for the shadows of prey above it.
When it spots something, it turns, and the eyes swing forward inside the shield to follow.
Scientists think it may even pick off food caught in the tentacles of siphonophores, the same group of drifting colonies as the man o' war.
Doug leans in for a closer look, and the barreleye rotates its eyes to look back at him,
